newsitem.title: GERMANY: High fishmeal prices discourage European uses.
newsitem.headline: High fishmeal prices discourage European uses.

text.p: Fishmeal demand will be slack in Europe as long as high prices make the protein-rich feed less attractive than competing meals and grains, Hamburg's grain/feeds association said on Wednesday.
"Key importing countries in Europe bought about 20 percent less fishmeal last year," the chairman of the association's fishmeal section, Eberhard Wienholt, said at an annual meeting.
He did not see lower prices in 1997 as long as major buyer China showed no signs of slackening interest.
China may buy one million tonnes in 1997 after 800,000 tonnes last year, which was up by 100,000 from 1995, to supply its expanding poultry, pig and fish farming sectors, he said.
German and European consumers had only taken limited cover up to the second quarter of 1997.
Although prices had last eased, they were still historically high -- a result of long fishing bans in Perus.
Fishmeal c&f Hamburg at the end of February was at $548 a tonne compared with a February average of $558 and $576 in January, data from the Oil World newsletter showed.
Wienholt estimated German net fishmeal consumption in 1996 at 120,000 tonnes, some 20 percent below the figure in 1995.
He said this illustrated the deterrent effect of high prices especially versus competing soymeal.
Gross fishmeal imports were estimated at least at par with 268,000 tonnes in 1995.
Germany serves as a transit point for fishmeal exports to other European Union and third countries including Hungary, the Czech and Slovak republics, Russia, Austria and Romania.
But Jan-Oct 1996 shipments to eastern Europe at 58,200 tonnes compared with 102,100 in full-year 1995 showed consumers there had reduced consumption due to high prices.
Wienholt also showed 1996 figures from the Paris-based fishmeal exporters' organisation FEO.
The 1996 combined output of 4.12 million tonnes in FEO member countries Chile, Peru, Denmark, Iceland and Norway was only marginally changed from 4.15 million in 1995.
FEO exports of 3.37 million tonnes in 1996 were down from 3.76 million in 1995, which he attributed to higher domestic consumption, for example in the Chilean poultry industry.
FEO countries exported 82 percent of their output (90 percent in 1995) and Asian countries received some 55 percent of the total. --Vera Eckert, Hamburg newsroom, +49-40-41903275
